name: vvdec (VVdeC)
baseline: FFmpeg native VVC decoder (FFVVC); also VTM and OpenVVC per the lead, but no numbers against them on opened pages
workload: Software H.266/VVC Main10 decoding of VTM-10.0 encoded JVET common-test-condition sequences (ClassA, ClassB; random access, all intra, low-delay P) on a Xeon workstation with 20 threads; the FFmpeg comparison is a qualitative statement on the wiki.
claimed_speedup: Wiki page 'Integration in FFmpeg' (opened): 'As VVdeC is still faster and realtime capable' than the VVC decoder built into FFmpeg; no ratio is given on that page. Wiki Home page performance chart (opened, values read off the plot so approximate, latest v2.2 points): about 299 fps RA ClassB, about 299 fps LBP ClassB, about 131 fps AI ClassB, about 79 fps RA ClassA, about 44 fps AI ClassA; the first release v0.1 started at about 233, 100, 65 and 32 fps for RA ClassB, AI ClassB, RA ClassA and AI ClassA.
hardware: Linux workstation with Xeon W-2155 @ 3.3 GHz, 20 threads (all cores)
stars_or_usage: 563 stars; integrated into FFmpeg (community libvvdec patchset) and mpv via wiki guides
tradeoffs: Decoder only. Supports all VVC Main10 features. Based on the VTM reference software with SIMD (x86, ARM via SIMDe, native ARM SIMD since v2.1) and task-level multi-threading. Safari/WebKit cannot run the WASM build. The FFmpeg integration is a community patch, not merged into FFmpeg master. The Clear BSD license states that no patent rights are granted, which matters for VVC.
caveats: No benchmark against a named competitor appears on any opened page: the wiki chart plots VVdeC against its own release history, and the FFmpeg comparison is a one-sentence assertion without numbers. The fps values above are read from a chart image (Home page, chart file dated 2024-02-05), not from a table. Snippet only (pages blocked in this environment, not opened): a FOSDEM 2024 handout by the FFmpeg VVC decoder author is reported by search snippets to say that FFVVC C code and multithreading are on par with VVdeC (VVdeC about 10 percent faster single-threaded on Linux, about 10 percent slower on Windows) and that VVdeC with asm was about 90 percent faster single-threaded and 75 percent faster multi-threaded than FFVVC at that time (early 2024, before FFmpeg added AVX2 VVC asm). The OpenVVC paper (arXiv 2205.12217, snippet only) is reported to say OpenVVC scales better than VVdeC with more threads and uses about half the memory. A retier from an environment that reaches archive.fosdem.org or arXiv could lift this to B.

name: soundkit (soundkit-opus)
baseline: libopus (Opus trunk commit 03647f524a40b05a1898522e92033810b58103c7, direct in-process C calls)
workload: Pure-Rust 48 kHz stereo CELT-only codec versus libopus: 5 ms (240-sample) frames, OPUS_APPLICATION_AUDIO, maximum complexity, 16-bit and 24-bit PCM, CBR and constrained VBR at 192/256/320 kb/s; four 10 s music excerpts, median of 3 alternating rounds with 7 repeats each, pinned to one CPU.
claimed_speedup: Encode: 1.19-2.36% less time than trunk libopus in all 12 aggregate cells (Rust 96.80-107.55x realtime; for example 16-bit CBR 192 kb/s 371.9126 ms versus 380.9057 ms, -2.36%). Decode, each implementation on its own packets: 1.50-4.64% less time, but the project withdrew this as the decoder gate; the same-packet 24-bit gate at 192 kb/s constrained VBR over 4 sources measured +0.51% (slower) on C packets, -0.30% on SoundKit packets, +0.10% combined, which the project calls native parity within noise. Perceptual score 4.5731 MOS-LQO versus 4.5724 for libopus trunk.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.97.1 release profile, ThinLTO, one codegen unit, -C target-cpu=native; C driver tools/raw_celt_bench.c built with GCC 12.2.0 -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native against static libopus.a from trunk
hardware: GCP c4-highcpu-4, 4 vCPU Intel Xeon Platinum 8581C (Emerald Rapids), Debian 12 x86-64, process pinned to CPU 2 with taskset
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; successor of the listed libopus-rs (moved into soundkit-opus 0.13.x on 2026-08-25, history kept)
tradeoffs: Safe public Rust API with checked wrappers around private unsafe SIMD kernels (SAFETY.md); no libopus FFI. Scope is narrow: 48 kHz CELT-only fullband mono/stereo; decoder rejects SILK, hybrid, FEC and mode transitions; no packet-loss concealment; production target is 5 ms stereo at 192-320 kb/s. CBR packet bytes match libopus but constrained-VBR streams differ (350-527 bytes per 400 s). Wasm path is not at parity: CODEC.md (Node.js, full track, 20 ms frames) reports Rust wasm encode at 127-128x realtime versus 147.4x for C libopusjs at 48 kb/s and 81-82x versus 110.9x at 128 kb/s, with Rust wasm decode faster at 48 kb/s (377-380x versus 332.5x) and slightly slower at 128 kb/s.
caveats: Margin is small (1-2 percent) and covers encode only; decode is parity once both decoders read identical packets. One x86 host, no AArch64 or Wasm parity claim. The four 100 s licensed music sources are not in the repository (the runner accepts another corpus via --corpus), the libopus configure string was not recorded, the final timing JSON records build-flag fields as unknown because binaries were reused, and the raw result JSON stays local; the report gives SHA-256 hashes only. Benchmark code is public (soundkit-opus/tools/run_soundkit_flac_corpus.py, raw_celt_bench.c, run_native_celt_ab.py, run_same_packet_decode_ab.py), so tier A follows the literal rule, but a verifier may cap it at C because of the private corpus. First-party results. Other soundkit crates carry stronger first-party claims against FFmpeg and other baselines that could be separate records: soundkit-alac README reports 13.51% less elapsed time than FFmpeg C ALAC decoding at 16-bit and 11.58% at 24-bit (20-file corpus, same Xeon 8581C host, thin LTO, target-cpu=native, byte-exact PCM); README table also states soundkit-vorbis 8.65% less elapsed time per sample than libvorbis C and soundkit-mp3 2.17% less time per sample than minimp3 C.

name: sst-basic-blocks LanczosResampler (Surge)
baseline: libsamplerate sinc resampling (SRC_SINC_FASTEST in the NonIntegerSRC harness); the issue says only 'Sinc interpolation'
workload: Third-party run of the NonIntegerSRC src_test harness: resampling a 1,000,000-sample 100 Hz sine at 48k to 96k, 96k to 48k, 44.1k to 48k and 48k to 44.1k in 2048-sample blocks, wall-clock timed with std::chrono, comparing libsamplerate, a Holters-Parker resampler and Surge's Lanczos resampler.
claimed_speedup: Issue 4 on NonIntegerSRC (opened 2026-05-18): 'I found out the Lanczos interpolation was faster by a factor of two on my machine'; no timings given.
license: MIT OR GPL-3.0-or-later (LanczosResampler.h is dual licensed; the rest of sst-basic-blocks is GPL-3.0-or-later)
stars_or_usage: 17 stars; described in its README as the bottom of the stack of the Surge libraries
tradeoffs: Small-window Lanczos (A=4, 8 taps) with a 8192-entry interpolated coefficient table and SSE intrinsics, built for 48 kHz to variable-rate use; the header needs sst simd setup and a sum_ps_to_float reduction (or hadd) when copied. Filter quality versus long sinc kernels is not measured in the evidence. Only the three listed headers are MIT; everything else needs GPL-3.0.
caveats: Only evidence is an unanswered user question in another repository: no CPU, compiler, flags, timings or baseline version, and it is not clear whether the compared 'Sinc' was libsamplerate or the Holters-Parker resampler. NonIntegerSRC vendors an older copy of the Surge resampler class (src_utils/LanczosResampler.h), not the sst-basic-blocks header; its libsamplerate wrapper runs one channel; its CMakeLists sets no build type or optimization flags (README builds with plain cmake -Bbuild, and --config Release only matters for multi-config generators), so a Linux default build may be unoptimized. The same README claims its Holters-Parker resampler is about 17-40x faster than libsamplerate (chart: 39.81x for 48k to 96k, 16.92x for 96k to 48k, 21.17x for 44.1k to 48k, 21.85x for 48k to 44.1k), which is far above the Lanczos 2x. No libsamplerate or r8brain comparison and no benchmark exist in sst-basic-blocks itself (README, tree and header read). A search snippet from another source ('Lanczos 4.5x slower than sinc_best, 2x faster than sinc_fastest') was not traced to a page I opened and is not used.
